text: Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) is the flag carrier of Pakistan, with its primary hub at Jinnah International Airport in Karachi, and secondary hubs at Allama Iqbal International Airport in Lahore and Islamabad International Airport. PIA was under the administrative control of the Secretary to the Government of Pakistan for Aviation until its privatization in 2025. The airline traces its origins to Orient Airways, founded on 29 October 1946 by Mirza Ahmad Ispahani and Adamjee Haji Dawood in Calcutta, British India, and became the first and only Muslim-owned airline in the British Raj. After Pakistan's independence on 14 August 1947, Orient Airways began relief operations and served routes between East and West Pakistan. In 1952, the government subsidized Orient Airways by purchasing three Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellations through a newly established subsidiary, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), at a cost of 25 million rupees. On 1 October 1953, Orient Airways and PIA were formally merged under the Pakistan International Airlines Corporation Ordinance, 1955, with the government taking majority control. The merged airline operated a fleet of three Super Constellations, two Convair CV-240s, and eleven DC-3s. On 11 March 1955, Orient Airways ceased operations. PIA inaugurated its first international route on 11 March 1955, flying from Karachi to London Heathrow via Cairo and Rome using Super Constellations, carrying 113,165 passengers in 1955—50% more than in 1954. In May 1956, PIA ordered five Vickers Viscount 815s and partnered with Pan Am to train personnel. Passenger numbers rose to 208,000 between 1957 and 1958, prompting the purchase of two additional Super Constellations. In February 1960, PIA wet-leased a Boeing 707 from Pan American Airlines and introduced it on the Karachi-London route on 7 March 1960, becoming the second Asian airline to operate a jet aircraft commercially, with an all-Pakistani crew beginning operations on 20 June 1960. By the end of 1960, PIA achieved financial profitability. On 5 May 1961, it launched its first trans-Atlantic route, Karachi to New York JFK via London, which was suspended in February 1963. In 1961, PIA ordered three Boeing 720s, delivered in 1962. On 2 January 1962, a PIA Boeing 720B set a world record speed of 938.78 km/h (582.98 mph) from London to Karachi, a record still held today. In 1963, Fokker F27 Friendships and Sikorsky helicopters were ordered; the latter served 20 towns in East Pakistan until 1966. In 1964, PIA began flying the Dhaka-Guangzhou-Shanghai route, becoming the first non-Communist airline to fly to China, and on 10 May 1964, became the first non-Soviet airline to offer flights to Europe via Moscow. During the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965, PIA's aircraft were used for military logistics. The Viscounts were phased out in 1966 and replaced by four Hawker Siddeley Tridents. PIA expanded its network in the 1960s, adding Dhahran in 1962, Cairo services resumed, and by 1966, Paris, Istanbul, Baghdad, Kuwait, Jeddah, and Nairobi were added. Bangkok was added in 1967, and Manila, Tokyo, and Damascus in 1969. On 11 May 1967, Air Marshal Asghar Khan announced that PIA had become the fifth largest profit-making airline in the world, carrying one million passengers annually. In July 1967, he announced plans to build 64-room hotels in Sylhet, Sargodha, Sukkur, Mohenjo-daro, Chitral, Gilgit, and Kaptai, and 88-room hotels in Khulna, Lyallpur, Multan, and Murree, with 20 cottages attached to the 644-room Kaptai Hotel, and 125-room hotels in Peshawar and Chittagong. These European-style motels, equipped with air conditioning, heating, parking, and swimming pools, were completed in 1970 and funded through private investment, with no government financial participation. A new holding company was established to attract domestic investment, and Pakistan Services Ltd. contributed significantly. Bechtel Corp. prepared the design and cost estimates, recommending standardized designs using local materials. On 3 December 1971, a French national's attempt to hijack a PIA flight from Paris to Karachi was thwarted by French security forces. Transatlantic flights to New York resumed in May 1972 with a European stopover. In 1972, PIA added Tripoli to its network following improved ties with Libya and leased two Boeing 707s to Yugoslav airline JAT (now Air Serbia). In 1973, PIA acquired McDonnell Douglas DC-10s to replace its Boeing 707-300s. Nur Khan was appointed PIA executive for a second term in 1974, and in 1974, PIA launched Pakistan International Cargo. In 1976, PIA leased its first two Boeing 747s from TAP Air Portugal. By 1976–7, PIA carried 2.2 million passengers, up from 698,000 in 1972–3, and revenues reached $134 million in July–December 1976. On 20 January 1978, a PIA Fokker 27 was hijacked en route to Karachi from Sukkur. PIA began providing technical and administrative assistance or leasing aircraft to foreign airlines including Air China, Air Malta, Choson Minhang (now Air Koryo), Philippine Airlines, Somali Airlines, and Yemenia. A PIA subsidiary also began offering hotel management services in the UAE. Political upheaval in Pakistan during the late 1970s negatively impacted PIA's operations. In the 1980s, PIA expanded operations with the opening of a cargo handling center at Karachi airport, duty-free shops, the first C and D safety checks on its fleet, and the introduction of its first Airbus A300B4-200. In 1981, PIA had nearly 24,000 employees, which declined to 20,000 by 1983, still maintaining the world's highest employee-to-aircraft ratio. Operations became increasingly decentralized during the early 1980s. PIA reported its highest ever profits in 1981–82 and again in 1983–84. In 1984, PIA introduced the Night Coach service as a low-cost domestic alternative. The PIA Planetarium was inaugurated in Karachi, followed by ones in Lahore and Peshawar, featuring retired PIA aircraft for educational use. Two retired Boeing 720B aircraft were donated to the Karachi and Lahore planetaria. PIA profits rose again in 1984–85. In June 1985, PIA became the first Asian airline to operate the Boeing 737-300, after six aircraft were delivered. PIA played a key role in establishing Emirates in 1985 by providing technical and administrative support, leasing a Boeing 737–300 and an Airbus A300B4-200. In late 1987 and early 1988, services to Malé, Manchester, and Toronto were introduced. Throughout the 1990s, PIA sustained operating losses and liquidity problems due to frequent pilot strikes, vendor issues, over-staffing, and political interference. In 1990, First Officer Maliha Sami became the first female pilot of PIA on the Karachi-Panjgur-Turbat-Gwadar route. In June 1991, PIA took delivery of its first of six Airbus A310-300s, introducing flights to Tashkent in 1992 and Zurich in 1993. In March 1993, AVM Farooq Umar became managing director. An Open Skies agreement between Karachi and Dubai was agreed upon in 1993, allowing 12 private airlines to operate domestically, which placed significant financial pressure on PIA. PIA operates a fleet of 32 aircraft, primarily Boeing 777 types, Airbus A320s, and ATR aircraft. It runs nearly 50 daily flights, serving 20 domestic and 28 international destinations across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North America. PIA operates a frequent flyer program called Awards +Plus and is not part of any airline alliance. The airline owns Sofitel Paris, The Scribe Hotel in Paris, and The Roosevelt Hotel in New York City, which is now used as a homeless shelter. The Government of Pakistan's 2020 report noted that after Air Marshals Nur Khan and Asghar Khan—whose leadership was regarded as the "Golden Age of PIA"—departed, the airline entered a downward trajectory, suffering billions in losses, with declining assets, escalating disciplinary issues, and unions indirectly taking control. Capable aircraft were grounded, and repairable equipment was neglected. From 30 June 2020 until 29 November 2024, PIA was banned from flying in European airspace after the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) determined it was not capable of certifying or overseeing its operations in accordance with international standards. This ban was also implemented in other non-EU territories after it was revealed that at least a fourth of all pilot licenses issued in Pakistan were not genuine. Following prolonged financial losses, governance issues, and international operational restrictions, PIA was privatized in 2025, ending direct government ownership and transferring majority control to the private sector.
